In the pre-independence period the British government deprived tribal people of their right to livelihood on forest resources, and this led to tribal uprisings — of the Kolam from Chota Nagpur, the Gond from Orissa, the Koli, Bhilla and Ramoshi from Maharashtra and the Santhal and Munda from Bihar.

The tribal struggle has continued since those years. Tribals in India still face several problems, and one major problem is that they are denied their right over forests.

The main demand of the tribal movement is that their right over forests should be accepted: they should be allowed to collect the products of forests and should also have the right to cultivate on forest land.

The labour movement in India emerged in the background of industrialisation, after the textile industry and the railway companies were established in India in the latter half of the nineteenth century.

In 1899 railway workers went on strike for their demands. The first organisation for resolving the issues of workers was established in 1920 and is known as the All India Trade Union Congress.

In the post-independence period the labour movement started working more effectively, and in the 1960s and 1970s it organised several agitations. But from the 1980s the labour movement started getting disintegrated, and globalisation has affected it to a great extent. Workers in India still face problems such as unstable employment conditions, contract labour, financial insecurity, absence of legal protection, unlimited working hours, insecurity at the workplace and health hazards.

Environmental degradation is a serious problem at both the national and the international level. At the international level several movements are working to stop the deterioration of the environment, and there is significant international cooperation in this field.

In India many movements are working on different aspects of the environment. The environment movements take up issues such as the protection of bio-diversity, protecting the different sources of water, the protection of forests and of the green belt, the pollution of rivers, and the use of chemicals and their ill effects.

The chapter's example of such work is Dr Rajendra Singh, also known as the 'Waterman of India', who brought a water revolution in Rajasthan. He became famous for building thousands of 'Johad' and revived rivers in the desert of Rajasthan. He formed an organisation, 'Tarun Bharat Sangh', which worked for building eleven thousand Johad in hundreds of villages, and all over India he started a campaign for water conservation, the revival of rivers, forest conservation and wild life conservation. His social movement has been active for the last 31 years, and he won the Stockholm Water Prize, an award known as the 'Nobel Prize for water'.

The farmers movement in India is an important movement. During the British period farmers started getting organised because of the anti-agriculture policies of the colonial government; the movements at Bardoli and Champaranya and the movements against revenue collection belong to this period, and they were inspired by the thoughts of Mahatma Phule, Justice Ranade and Mahatma Gandhi.

After independence, some reforms in agriculture — tenancy laws and laws relating to the tilling of the land — slowed the movement down. It became more active and effective again after the Green Revolution. Although the Green Revolution aimed at increasing agricultural production and achieving self-sufficiency in food grains, it did not benefit the poor farmers; the farmers were now divided into rich farmers and poor farmers, and the dissatisfaction among the poor farmers led to the beginning of the farmer's movement in its later form.

Appropriate price for agricultural products, agriculture to be treated as an industry, implementation of the recommendations of the Swaminathan Commission, debt relief, debt cancellation and a national policy for agriculture are some of the demands of the farmers movement. Shetkari Sanghatana, Bharatiya Kisan Union and All India Kisan Sabha are some of the important farmers organisations in India.

In the pre-independence period progressive men in India initiated the women's movement. It aimed at eliminating injustice against women and ending their exploitation, at helping them to lead a respectful life and at enabling them to participate actively in social life. The movement aimed at the freedom of women, and demanded that women should be treated as human beings.

Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar, Raja Rammohan Roy, Mahatma Jyotirao Phule, Savitribai Phule, Maharshee Dhondo Keshav Karve, Pandita Ramabai and Ramabai Ranade took the initiative in ending the practice of Sati and of child marriages.

Reforms such as widow remarriage, women's education and the right to vote for women were made possible by the work of these reformists.

Political parties compete for political power, win elections and try to resolve the problems of the common people, but they must adopt a comprehensive perspective — from public cleanliness to space research they have to consider all matters from a national point of view and have a programme for all sections of society. They cannot concentrate on just one particular issue.

A movement can. It is a collective action in which people's active participation is expected, and it is formed when people come together in the interest of a particular issue, with a particular social objective or a focussed problem. Movements therefore bring to attention the issues that a party's comprehensive programme cannot concentrate on, and the chapter says the movements increase the participation of people in public life. That is why movements are important in a democracy.

False.

The chapter lists leadership among the features of a movement. Movements have a leadership, and the leadership keeps the movement active. The objectives of the movement, its programme of action and its strategy of agitation are all decided by its leaders.

The chapter states directly that a strong leadership makes a movement effective, so a movement does need strong leadership.

True.

The consumer movement emerged in India after the Consumer Protection Act came into existence in 1986.

The movement has a broad objective and believes that each member of society is a consumer. Because of the changing nature of the social and economic system, consumers face different problems such as adulteration, increased cost of items and frauds in weights and measures, and the consumer movement works to protect consumers from such frauds.

[Note: unlike the other two statements in this question, this one makes no claim that could be judged right or wrong — it only says that the consumer movement exists, which the chapter states outright — so it appears to be an incomplete sentence in the printed exercise.]
